topics.summary: You are not just you: you are a walking city. About as many bacterial cells live in and on your body as your own cells (scientists used to say 10 times more, until a 2016 study corrected it). Your gut microbes help digest food and make vitamins; skin microbes guard against germs. Deeper still, the tiny power stations inside every cell, mitochondria, were once separate bacteria that moved in and never left. Lynn Margulis proposed this and was ridiculed for years before scientists accepted it. Even our DNA carries leftover pieces of ancient viruses. So which part is 'me'?
topics.oneness: If half the cells in my body are not 'mine', and my energy comes from ancient bacteria, what is 'I'?

topics.name: My genes
sub: Every cell carries instructions (DNA), like a recipe book

topics.summary: Inside almost every cell is a long coded message called DNA, a recipe book for building and running a body. We extract real DNA from strawberries and see the white strands. Half our recipes come from each biological parent, mixed in a new way, which is why siblings look alike but different. All living things use the same four DNA letters, so we share many genes even with bananas. We meet Mendel, a monk whose pea experiments were ignored for 34 years; Rosalind Franklin, whose photo revealed DNA's shape but who got little credit; and Har Gobind Khorana, born in Punjab, who won a Nobel Prize for cracking how DNA's code works. And we learn that genes are not destiny: what we eat, how we live and how we are cared for changes which genes are used.
topics.oneness: If a banana and I share the same code, are we written in the same language by the same author?

sub: Life changed over billions of years (evolution): fish → amphibians → reptiles → mammals → primates → humans, a branching tree, not a ladder
Darwin and Wallace: natural selection
Other humans: Homo erectus, Neanderthals, Denisovans; Homo sapiens appear about 300,000 years ago in Africa
Many of us carry a little Neanderthal DNA
People reached India tens of thousands of years ago; Bhimbetka rock shelters
topics.summary: We follow our family line back through time: fish that crawled onto land, early mammals scurrying under dinosaurs, tree-climbing primates, and many kinds of humans, several of them alive at the same time. Darwin and Wallace explained how living things slowly change: those best suited to their surroundings survive and pass on their traits. We see that evolution is a branching bush, not a ladder, and that new fossils keep pushing dates back. We visit (in pictures or in person) Bhimbetka's rock paintings, among the oldest human art in India. Then we compare this with the Dashavatara: Matsya (fish), Kurma (tortoise), Varaha (boar), Narasimha (half-lion, half-human), Vamana (small human), then full humans. Many people see in this order a story that parallels evolution.
topics.oneness: If all life is one family tree, is there anyone who is not my relative?

res.title: The Story of Life: Evolution, Catherine Barr & Steve Williams
Bhimbetka rock shelters (Madhya Pradesh)

topics.name: What's common between me and other life?
sub: Me & a dog: mammals, backbone, the same organs, hair, milk, feelings
Me & a bird: backbone, lungs, a 4-chambered heart
Me & a fish: backbone; early embryos look alike
Me & a tree: cells, DNA, using energy, water
Me & a mushroom: closer relatives than plants
Me & bacteria: the same DNA code and energy molecule
Differences too
topics.summary: We play detective comparing ourselves with other beings, one at a time. A dog shares our skeleton plan, organs, fur-like hair, milk-feeding and clearly feels joy and fear. A bird has a 4-chambered heart like ours. A tree breathes at the level of its cells, carries DNA and is made of cells like us. Even bacteria run on the same genetic code and energy molecule. The deeper we look, the longer the 'same' list grows. We also hear the 2012 Cambridge Declaration on Consciousness, in which scientists stated that many animals, including birds and octopuses, are conscious, and the 2024 New York Declaration, which says even insects might be.
topics.oneness: 'Tat tvam asi': you are that. When does 'same' become 'one'?

res.title: My Octopus Teacher (2020)

topics.name: Our closest cousins
sub: Great apes: chimpanzees and bonobos (closest; about 98–99% similar DNA), gorillas, orangutans
Monkeys and other primates
India's only ape: the hoolock gibbon (Northeast)
Shared: tools, emotions, play, laughter, culture
Jane Goodall: chimps use tools
topics.summary: Chimpanzees and bonobos are our closest living relatives; we shared an ancestor several million years ago. When Jane Goodall saw a chimp stripping a twig to fish for termites, scientists had believed tool-making was what made humans unique. Her mentor Louis Leakey said we must now 'redefine tool, redefine man, or accept chimpanzees as humans.' Chimps laugh, mourn, make up after fights and have local traditions. India has its own ape, the hoolock gibbon, singing in northeastern forests. We tape our thumbs to see why our hands matter, and ask: what, if anything, makes humans special?
topics.oneness: Every 'only humans can…' claim has been challenged. Is the line between us and them real?

res.title: Jane Goodall documentaries (e.g. Jane, 2017)

topics.name: My family history
sub: Family tree (3 generations); 'family' = the people who raise and love me (inclusive of adopted, single-parent and other families)
Traits that run in families: face, height, hair, handedness
Fingerprints: unique, even for identical twins
Stories, languages, places, recipes
How long people lived then vs now
Blood groups and family illnesses: parent-led and kept light
topics.summary: Every child is the newest page in a very long story. We build a family tree, interview a grandparent or elder, collect photos and stories, and look at what is shared: a nose, a laugh, a love of cooking. We take fingerprints and discover that no two people, not even identical twins, have the same ones. We learn that in 1947 people in India lived on average only about 32 years and now about 70, and ask why. For families that wish to, parents can add blood groups and health stories. Families made by adoption or in other ways trace both their 'raised-by' and 'born-from' stories in whatever way feels right.
topics.oneness: My family tree joins every other family tree if I go back far enough. Where does my family end?

topics.name: My body parts
sub: Skin (the largest organ), bones (about 300 at birth, 206 in adults), muscles, heart, lungs, stomach and intestines, brain
How they work together
Why they evolved: forward eyes, gripping thumbs, sweating for long-distance running, goosebumps from furry ancestors, tailbone
The appendix: once called useless, now possibly a store of helpful microbes
topics.summary: We trace the child's body on a big sheet of paper and place cut-out organs inside. We listen to the heart with a home-made stethoscope before and after jumping, blow up a balloon to feel lung power, and build a moving finger from straws and string. Then we ask 'why do I have this?' Goosebumps are left over from furry ancestors whose hair stood up; sweating lets humans run for hours; babies are born with about 300 bones that fuse to 206. We learn that science changes its mind: the appendix was called useless for a century and now may be a safe house for helpful gut microbes. Finally we meet another way of seeing the body: Sushruta, an early surgeon who described nose reconstruction, and the yoga and Ayurveda traditions that describe the body differently.
topics.oneness: My heart beats without my asking. Is it 'my' heart, or is it doing its own thing?

res.title: Science centres: Nehru Science Centre Mumbai, Visvesvaraya Museum Bengaluru, National Science Centre Delhi

topics.name: My body's sensors
sub: Beyond the 'five senses': touch, pressure, vibration, temperature, pain, itch, balance, body position (eyes closed), hunger, thirst, full tummy, heartbeat, the urge to breathe
Conscious vs automatic sensing
Senses mix: flavour = taste + smell
Other beings: birds (UV, magnetic field), bees (UV), snakes (heat), sharks (electric fields), bats (echoes), dogs (smell)
Plants sense light, gravity and touch
topics.summary: Aristotle listed five senses over 2000 years ago, and people repeated the list ever since. But your body is covered in sensors: you know where your hand is with your eyes closed, you feel hot and cold, you stay balanced on one foot, you feel hungry, thirsty or that you need the toilet, and a hidden sensor makes you breathe faster when you run. Scientists today count anywhere from about 20 to over 30 senses and still disagree on how to count. We pinch our noses and find apple and potato taste almost the same, because most flavour is smell. Then we meet the superpowers of others: snakes 'see' heat, sharks feel electricity, bats hear their way in the dark, birds feel Earth's magnetism. Even plants sense: roots know which way is down and the touch-me-not folds when touched.
topics.oneness: If a plant senses touch and I sense touch, is sensing the beginning of awareness everywhere?

res.title: What If You Had Animal Eyes?, Sandra Markle

topics.name: How do I think?
sub: The brain: about 86 billion neurons sending signals
Thinking = patterns of signals; learning changes connections
Memory: short-term and long-term; sleep helps memory; memories change each time we recall them
Emotions affect thinking
Other thinkers: crows, octopuses; even brainless slime moulds solve mazes
The hard question: how does the brain make experience?
topics.summary: Your brain has about 86 billion nerve cells passing tiny electric and chemical signals; every time you learn something new, the connections change. We play memory games and discover tricks that help (stories, pictures, a 'memory palace' walk through the house) and learn that sleep is when the brain files memories. Surprisingly, a memory changes a little each time you remember it. Thinking isn't only human: crows plan, octopuses solve puzzles, and a slime mould with no brain at all can find the shortest path through a maze. Then the biggest mystery: nobody knows how signals in the brain become the feeling of being you. Some scientists say the mind is what the brain does; Vedanta says consciousness comes first and the brain is something that appears within it.
topics.oneness: Who is watching my thoughts? Is the watcher a thought too?

topics.name: Getting sick, getting hurt & getting well
sub: Why we get sick: germs (bacteria, viruses), not enough food or sleep, allergies
The body's defences: skin, mucus, fever, white blood cells, antibodies, immune memory (how vaccines work)
Hygiene habits: handwashing (20 seconds), teeth, bathing, clean water and food, covering coughs
Getting hurt: cuts, burns, falls, electric shock; electricity safety at home
Healing: scabs, rest
Are 'I' and 'my body' different?
topics.summary: We learn that the body is a fortress: skin is the wall, mucus is a sticky trap, fever is the body turning up the heat on germs, and white blood cells are guards who remember invaders so they can fight faster next time (which is how vaccines work). Glitter 'germs' show why handwashing matters, and bread touched by washed vs unwashed hands grows very different mould. We tell the story of Dr Semmelweis, who told doctors to wash their hands in the 1840s and was mocked; years later germ theory proved him right. We learn home safety, especially electricity: water and electricity never mix, never touch sockets or bare wires, and never touch someone being shocked; switch off first. Finally the question: we say 'help my body heal'. Who is helping whom? Am I my body, or something more?
topics.oneness: When I say 'my body', who is the 'I' that owns it?

res.title: Germs Make Me Sick!, Melvin Berger

topics.name: What is food?
sub: Food = building material + energy + helpers (vitamins, minerals) + water
Digestion breaks food down: proteins → amino acids, carbohydrates → sugars, fats → fatty acids
All life uses the same ~20 amino acids, DNA code and energy molecule (ATP)
So why so many foods? Different bodies have different tools (teeth, enzymes, gut microbes)
Plants make their own food from light; food chains
Food for different beings: cows (helped by microbes), spiders, plants, fungi
topics.summary: We chew a piece of plain roti for two minutes and it starts tasting sweet: saliva is already breaking starch into sugar. Digestion is a giant breaking-down factory: proteins become amino acids, carbohydrates become sugars, fats become fatty acids, and the body rebuilds them into itself. Amazingly, every living thing builds itself from the same 20 or so amino acids. So why does a cow eat grass, a spider eat flies and a plant eat sunlight? Because each has different tools: a cow's stomach is full of microbes that break down grass, which we cannot do. We also learn that nutrition science keeps changing its mind: fat was the villain, then sugar, and eggs went from bad to fine.
topics.oneness: 'Annam Brahma': food is the Absolute. When I eat a mango, does the mango become me, or do I become a little more mango?

res.title: StoryWeaver: food stories

topics.name: Energy beyond food
sub: Sunlight: plants make sugar from light (photosynthesis); we make vitamin D in sunlight; warmth
Air: oxygen helps cells release energy from food; we breathe out carbon dioxide
Water: most of the body is water; every cell works in it
Life without sunlight: deep-sea vents where bacteria make food from chemicals (chemosynthesis); tubeworms
Microbes that 'breathe' nitrate or sulphate instead of oxygen; life in boiling springs, ice and deep rock
Tardigrades survive extremes
topics.summary: Food is only one kind of fuel. Plants catch sunlight and turn it into sugar; that sugar feeds almost everything else, including us. Our cells use oxygen to release energy from food, like a slow fire, and we breathe out carbon dioxide. A plant left in a dark box turns pale, and a candle under a jar goes out when its oxygen runs low. Then we dive to the deep ocean floor, where no sunlight has ever reached, and find whole communities living on chemicals from hot volcanic vents. Some microbes breathe sulphate instead of oxygen, some live in boiling water or deep inside rocks, and tiny tardigrades can survive drying out and even the vacuum of space. Life is far stranger and more flexible than the textbook picture.
topics.oneness: If all my energy started as sunlight, am I a little bit of the Sun, walking around?
